attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: Keeps 'vast majority', the 'mostly' qualifier and his statement that demand exists. The 'cannot afford long-term' clause is a forward judgment with no horizon. The contract rightly leaves it unscored.

contract.note: The plain reading of 'vast majority' as well over half of demand by end buyer is ordinary and fair. Using H1 2026 as the period is reasonable. The open question of whether Meta counts as buying for the labs is flagged, so the result depends on that interpretation.

evidence.note: April 2026 report of Meta's $21B dedicated-capacity commitment to CoreWeave. It shows a large hyperscaler buyer, but it does not give the end use or any shares of total demand.
Jane Street's roughly $6B CoreWeave commitment in April 2026 shows some demand from outside the named group. One deal does not establish shares of overall demand.

reviews.rationale: The claim needs shares of AI compute demand by end buyer and the end use of hyperscaler-bought capacity. The packet has neither. Meta's and Jane Street's deals suggest some large buying outside OpenAI and Anthropic, but they do not show the shares. The packet's own gaps confirm this. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, rebutting an investor assumption that he names, in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps his 'I can find' scope limit and his exact list. 'I can find' limits the scope of his search. It is not a probability hedge, so the claim stays scoreable.

contract.note: The contract tests the rebuttal of 'all have locked-in demand' and checks his list loosely. That is a fair, ordinary reading of his words. Reading 'locked-in' as signed leases or offtakes is reasonable. CBRE covers all data centers, not only AI ones, and that limit is flagged.

evidence.note: CBRE H1 2026 data, published Aug 2026 before the evaluation date: just over 80% of capacity under construction is preleased, leaving up to about 1,500 MW without a tenant. So not all capacity is locked in. The data cover all data centers in primary markets, not only AI.

June 2026 industry piece naming AI campuses built ahead of named tenants or without disclosed preleasing (Delta Forge 1, CloudBurst). Some dollar figures are garbled, but the text is readable and relevant.
SemiAnalysis says long-term offtakes are dominated by AI labs, often backstopped by hyperscalers. This fits his description of where committed demand comes from. It is background only.

reviews.rationale: In H1 2026 about a fifth of North American capacity under construction had no tenant (CBRE), and named AI campuses were built on spec (Build). So the assumption that all AI data centers have locked-in demand was untrue. SemiAnalysis supports his account that committed offtakes come mainly from AI labs and hyperscalers. The packet shows no broad set of committed customers outside his list. Supported on the contract's reading.
